museums.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
museums.desc: The Met is the largest art museum in the Americas, with more than two million works, from ancient Egyptian temples to Van Gogh and modern design. It stands on the edge of Central Park on Fifth Avenue and welcomes millions of visitors every year.
museums.history: A group of New York citizens, businessmen and artists founded the Met in 1870, after a speech in Paris in 1866 that argued America should have a great art museum of its own. It opened in a rented building in 1872 and moved to its current home in Central Park in 1880. The grand Fifth Avenue entrance was added in the early 1900s, and in 1965 the museum even rebuilt an Egyptian temple, the Temple of Dendur, inside a glass hall. Over time rich collectors donated whole collections, so today it is like several museums in one.

highlights.title: Aristotle with a Bust of Homer

museums.name: Museum of Modern Art (MoMA)
museums.desc: MoMA is the world's best-known museum of modern art, home to Van Gogh's Starry Night, Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, Dalí's melting clocks and Warhol's soup cans. It covers painting, sculpture, photography, design and film from the 1880s to today.
museums.history: MoMA was founded in 1929 by three women, Abby Aldrich Rockefeller, Lillie P. Bliss and Mary Quinn Sullivan, who wanted a museum for the new art that other museums ignored. It opened just nine days after the stock market crash of 1929, in a rented space in an office building. Its first director, Alfred H. Barr Jr., built a collection that included film and design as well as painting, which was new at the time. MoMA moved to its present site on West 53rd Street in 1939 and has been expanded several times since.

museums.name: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum
museums.desc: A white spiral building by the architect Frank Lloyd Wright houses a world-famous collection of modern art, especially abstract painting by Kandinsky and his circle. Visitors walk up a gentle ramp that winds around a huge open space.
museums.history: The collector Solomon R. Guggenheim began his foundation in 1937 to show 'non-objective' painting, art made of color and shape instead of recognizable things. His adviser, the artist Hilla Rebay, urged him to build a museum, and he hired Frank Lloyd Wright in 1943. The building took 16 years and opened in October 1959, shortly after both men had died. Its spiral shape was controversial at first and is now one of the most beloved buildings in New York.

museums.name: The Frick Collection
museums.desc: A steel tycoon's elegant mansion on Fifth Avenue is now a small museum filled with Old Master paintings by Vermeer, Rembrandt, Holbein and Titian. Because the rooms look like a home, it feels far more personal than a big museum.
museums.history: Henry Clay Frick, a Pittsburgh industrialist, built the mansion in 1913 to 1914 and filled it with art. When he died in 1919 he left it to the public, and after his widow Adelaide's death it opened as a museum in 1935. The rooms are still arranged much as the family lived in them, with paintings hung over fireplaces and among furniture. The result feels like a time capsule of Gilded Age taste.

museums.name: Art Institute of Chicago
museums.desc: Chicago's great museum, guarded by two bronze lions, holds some of the most famous paintings in America: Seurat's dotted Sunday on La Grande Jatte, Hopper's Nighthawks and Grant Wood's American Gothic. Its Impressionist collection is one of the best outside Paris.
museums.history: The Art Institute started in 1879 as a school and exhibition space for artists, and its current Beaux-Arts building on Michigan Avenue opened in 1893 for the World's Columbian Exposition. Wealthy Chicagoans, like Bertha Palmer, bought French Impressionist paintings early, before they were famous, and gave them to the museum. The Modern Wing, designed by Renzo Piano, opened in 2009. The bronze lions out front have been there since 1894, and they are dressed up in team gear when Chicago teams make the playoffs.

highlights.title: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte

museums.name: National Gallery of Art
museums.desc: Along the National Mall, this free museum holds the only painting by Leonardo da Vinci in the Americas, as well as great works by Vermeer, Rembrandt, Monet, Cole and many American artists. It is made up of an old marble building and a modern East Building joined by a tunnel with a moving walkway.
museums.history: The National Gallery was founded by an act of Congress in 1937 after the banker and Treasury Secretary Andrew W. Mellon offered his great art collection and money for a building to the American people. The neoclassical West Building opened in 1941. Mellon wanted a national collection that was not controlled by the government of the day, and he asked that the museum not carry his name. The East Building, designed by I. M. Pei, opened in 1978. Entry is free.

museums.name: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston
museums.desc: One of the largest art museums in the United States, with huge collections of Egyptian, Greek and Asian art and a famous collection of American paintings by Copley, Sargent and Homer. It also has one of the largest collections of Monet outside France.
museums.history: The MFA was founded in 1870, the same year as the Met, by Boston citizens, and opened in 1876 in Copley Square. By the 1900s it had outgrown its building and moved to its current home on Huntington Avenue in 1909. It has long sent archaeologists abroad, so its Egyptian collection is one of the best outside Cairo.

highlights.title: The Daughters of Edward Darley Boit
Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?

museums.name: Philadelphia Museum of Art
museums.desc: A Greek-temple-style museum at the top of a famous flight of steps, which the movie hero Rocky runs up. Inside are Van Gogh's Sunflowers, Cézanne's huge Bathers, Duchamp's Nude Descending a Staircase and a whole collection of Klee's strange, playful paintings.
museums.history: The museum began in 1876 when Philadelphia held the great Centennial Exhibition for the nation's 100th birthday. The city decided to make a permanent art museum from it. The Greek-revival building on a hill at the end of the Benjamin Franklin Parkway was begun in 1919 and opened in 1928. The museum's modern collections grew with the gifts of Louise and Walter Arensberg, who had known Marcel Duchamp personally.

museums.name: J. Paul Getty Museum (Getty Center)
museums.desc: A white hilltop campus above Los Angeles holds Van Gogh's Irises, Monet, Rembrandt and a superb collection of illuminated medieval manuscripts. The gardens and the views over the city are part of the visit, and entry is free.
museums.history: Oil tycoon J. Paul Getty opened a small museum in his ranch house in Malibu in 1954, then built a Roman-villa-style museum there in 1974. When he died in 1976 he left it a fortune, and the Getty Trust became one of the richest art institutions in the world. The new Getty Center, by architect Richard Meier, opened on a hilltop in Brentwood in 1997. The Malibu villa reopened in 2006 as the Getty Villa for classical antiquities.

aliases: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
museums.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
museums.desc: The largest art museum in the western United States, with art from all over the world and from every era. Outside its entrance is Urban Light, a forest of 202 restored antique street lamps that has become a symbol of Los Angeles.
museums.history: LACMA opened in 1965 on Wilshire Boulevard in an area called Miracle Mile, after it separated from the older Los Angeles County Museum of History, Science and Art, founded in 1910. Its first collections were helped by large gifts from wealthy collectors and Hollywood figures. The museum added the Pavilion for Japanese Art, the Broad Contemporary Art Museum and the glittering Urban Light in 2008. A new building is being constructed across the street.

highlights.title: The Treachery of Images (This is Not a Pipe)

museums.name: Cleveland Museum of Art
museums.desc: A free museum with one of the finest collections in the Midwest, from ancient Egypt to Monet, with a very strong collection of Asian art and Old Masters. Its marble building sits beside a lagoon in University Circle.
museums.history: Cleveland's industrialists left money for the museum in their wills in 1913, and the Greek-style marble building on a hill above Wade Lagoon opened in 1916. Its early directors were determined to buy only top-quality works. Admission has been free since the museum opened. In 2008 the museum began a huge rebuilding and expansion that brought a new glass atrium.

highlights.title: The Large Plane Trees (Road Menders at Saint-Rémy)

museums.name: Detroit Institute of Arts
museums.desc: The DIA is famous for Diego Rivera's huge murals about Detroit's factories, painted straight on the walls of its central court, and for a fine collection that includes Van Gogh and Bruegel.
museums.history: The museum started in 1885 when Detroit citizens founded the Detroit Museum of Art, and its current Beaux-Arts building opened in 1927. In 1932 and 1933 the Mexican artist Diego Rivera spent months painting the Detroit Industry murals, a salute to the city's car workers. When the city of Detroit went bankrupt in 2013, there was a danger that the art might be sold, but donors raised money to protect it in the 'Grand Bargain'.

museums.name: Barnes Foundation
museums.desc: One of the world's finest collections of Impressionist and early Modern art, including nearly 180 works by Renoir, 69 by Cézanne and Matisse's big mural, hung salon-style on the walls, just as the founder arranged them.
museums.history: The chemist and businessman Albert C. Barnes, who made a fortune with a medicine called Argyrol, began collecting in 1912 and founded the Barnes Foundation in 1922 as a school, not just a museum. He hung his pictures in groups with African art, furniture and metalwork to teach how to see. After his death in 1951 the collection stayed in Merion, Pennsylvania, until 2012, when it was moved to a new building in Philadelphia, which copied the arrangement of the rooms exactly.

highlights.title: The Joy of Life (Le bonheur de vivre)

museums.name: National Gallery of Canada
museums.desc: Canada's national art museum, in a glass-towered building overlooking the Ottawa River, holds the country's finest collection of Canadian art, including Tom Thomson's Jack Pine and many works by the Group of Seven, as well as European and Indigenous art. A giant spider sculpture called Maman stands outside.
museums.history: The Marquess of Lorne, Canada's Governor General, started the National Gallery in 1880 as part of the founding of the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts. The collection moved many times in its first century. Its present building, by the architect Moshe Safdie, opened in 1988. In 1913 the government gave the gallery its own law, and its great purchases of the 1910s and 1920s were of early Canadian painters such as Tom Thomson and the Group of Seven.

museums.name: Art Gallery of Ontario
museums.desc: Toronto's art gallery has a spiral staircase and a glass front designed by Frank Gehry, a big Canadian collection including Tom Thomson's West Wind, and the world's largest public collection of Henry Moore sculptures.
museums.history: It began in 1900 as the Art Museum of Toronto and became the Art Gallery of Toronto in 1919 and, in 1966, the Art Gallery of Ontario. Its first building was the Grange, an old mansion, and the gallery grew around it. In 2008 the architect Frank Gehry, who was born in Toronto, completed a big redesign. Its famous Canadian paintings came in part from Group of Seven supporters like J. S. McLean.

museums.name: Montreal Museum of Fine Arts
museums.desc: Canada's oldest art museum is made of several linked buildings on Sherbrooke Street in Montreal, with Canadian, European, Indigenous and decorative art, including some of the best Quebec paintings.
museums.history: The Art Association of Montreal was founded in 1860, making it the oldest art museum in Canada, and it opened its first gallery building on Phillips Square in 1879. The marble Beaux-Arts building on Sherbrooke Street opened in 1912, and several pavilions have been added since. It became known for large exhibitions, and its education programs for children and for people who are ill are well known.

museums.name: McMichael Canadian Art Collection
museums.desc: A log-and-stone gallery in the woods north of Toronto devoted to the Group of Seven and their circle, including a cabin shack that belonged to Tom Thomson and the graves of several of the painters.
museums.history: Robert and Signe McMichael began collecting Group of Seven paintings in the 1950s and in 1966 gave their log-and-stone house and 194 paintings to the province of Ontario, so that everyone could see the art in the setting that had inspired it. The collection now holds thousands of works, including Indigenous and Inuit art. Tom Thomson's own shack was moved to the grounds in 1962.

museums.name: Vancouver Art Gallery
museums.desc: British Columbia's main art museum, in a grand former courthouse in the middle of downtown Vancouver, holds the world's largest collection of work by the painter Emily Carr.
museums.history: The Vancouver Art Gallery opened in 1931 in a small building and moved to the old provincial courthouse, a neoclassical building redone by the architect Arthur Erickson, in 1983. Its collection of Emily Carr's paintings of Indigenous villages and wild forests came largely through gifts. A new building has been planned for decades.

museums.name: Canadian War Museum
museums.desc: Canada's national museum of military history holds the country's war art, including large paintings by official war artists of both World Wars. Its building by the Ottawa River is shaped like a grass-roofed bunker.
museums.history: The roots of the museum go back to 1880, when a small collection of war trophies began to be gathered in Ottawa. In 1916 the newspaper owner Lord Beaverbrook started the Canadian War Memorials Fund, hiring painters including A. Y. Jackson and Frederick Varley to record the First World War, and this is the core of the art collection. The museum moved to a dramatic new building designed by Raymond Moriyama in 2005.

aliases: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec
museums.name: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec
museums.desc: Quebec's national fine arts museum, set on the Plains of Abraham, tells the story of Quebec's art from the colonial period to today, with the largest collection of Quebec art in the world.
museums.history: The museum opened in 1933 as the Musée du Québec, in a neoclassical building on the Plains of Abraham, the very battlefield of 1759. It has been expanded several times, with new pavilions in 2002 and 2016. It is known for paintings by Cornelius Krieghoff, Jean Paul Lemieux and Jean Paul Riopelle.

museums.name: Museo Nacional de Arte (MUNAL)
museums.desc: Mexico's national art museum, in a lavish palace in the old center of Mexico City, shows five centuries of Mexican art, including the glowing volcano landscapes of José María Velasco.
museums.history: The museum was founded in 1982 and moved into the Palacio de Comunicaciones, a grand marble building finished in 1911 for the Mexican postal and telegraph service. The collection includes paintings from the colonial period to the early twentieth century. It's best known for landscapes of the Valley of Mexico by José María Velasco and works by Saturnino Herrán.

museums.name: Palacio de Bellas Artes
museums.desc: A white marble and stained glass palace in Mexico City, famous as an opera and concert hall and for huge murals by Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros on its walls.
museums.history: Mexico began the Palace of Fine Arts under President Porfirio Díaz in 1904, but the revolution interrupted construction and it was not opened until 1934. The building mixes Art Nouveau and Art Deco, and after the revolution the government invited the Mexican muralists to paint the walls. Rivera's Man at the Crossroads was painted for Rockefeller Center in New York, destroyed there, and repainted here in 1934.

aliases: National Museum of Fine Arts, Argentina
museums.name: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes
museums.desc: Argentina's national art museum, in the elegant Recoleta district of Buenos Aires, has the best collection of European art in South America as well as Argentine masters.
museums.history: Founded in 1895 by the art critic Eduardo Schiaffino, it was first housed in a department store building. Its present building, once a water pumping station, was remodeled in 1933 for the museum. It holds works by Goya, Monet, Rodin and Van Gogh next to the best of Argentine painters.

museums.name: São Paulo Museum of Art (MASP)
museums.desc: MASP is the most important art museum in Brazil's biggest city, in a famous red concrete building lifted on two giant beams over an open public square. It holds the best collection of European art in the southern hemisphere.
museums.history: The newspaper owner Assis Chateaubriand and the Italian art dealer Pietro Maria Bardi founded MASP in 1947 and gathered masterpieces by pressing wealthy Brazilians to donate. Its dramatic building on Paulista Avenue, designed by Lina Bo Bardi, opened in 1968. Its glass easels, which let visitors see paintings floating in the air without walls, became famous.

museums.name: Museu Nacional de Belas Artes
museums.desc: Brazil's national fine arts museum, in a classical building downtown, holds the best Brazilian painting of the 1800s, including big history paintings by Pedro Américo and Victor Meirelles.
museums.history: The museum was formally created in 1937 from the old National School of Fine Arts, which had been set up by French artists who came to Rio in 1816, after the Portuguese court had moved to Brazil. Its home, built in 1908, is a copy of a Parisian beaux-arts palace. It is known for its Brazilian academic painting of the 1800s.

museums.name: Museo de Arte de Lima (MALI)
museums.desc: Peru's main art museum shows 3,000 years of Peruvian art, from pre-Inca ceramics to colonial paintings, in a palace built for the 1872 Lima Exhibition.
museums.history: The museum opened in 1961 in the Palacio de la Exposición, a stately building from the 1870s in Lima's Parque de la Exposición. Its collection runs from ancient Paracas and Nazca textiles to Peruvian modern painters. It has a famous collection of colonial religious painting from the Cusco school.

museums.name: Louvre Museum
museums.desc: The most visited art museum in the world is housed in a former royal palace in the heart of Paris, with a glass pyramid in its courtyard. It holds the Mona Lisa, the Venus de Milo and more than 30,000 works from ancient times to the 1800s.
museums.history: The Louvre began as a fortress in about 1190, built by King Philip II to defend Paris. It was rebuilt as a royal palace in the 1500s, and King Louis XIV moved to Versailles in 1682, leaving the old palace to artists and scholars. After the French Revolution, the new government opened it as a public museum in 1793, with royal and church treasures that now belonged to the nation. Napoleon filled it with art from his conquests, much of which had to be returned in 1815. The glass pyramid by I. M. Pei, which serves as the main entrance, opened in 1989.

museums.name: Musée d'Orsay
museums.desc: A former railway station beside the Seine, with a giant clock, is now the home of the world's greatest collection of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist paintings by Monet, Renoir, Degas, Cézanne, Van Gogh and Gauguin.
museums.history: The Gare d'Orsay was built for the Paris World's Fair of 1900 and was the grandest railway station in the city. By the 1930s the platforms were too short for modern trains and the station fell out of use. It was saved from demolition in the 1970s and was turned into a museum for art from 1848 to 1914, which opened in 1986. The architects kept the huge iron and glass roof and the great station clock, which you can look through from the fifth floor.

highlights.title: Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette
The Starry Night Over the Rhône

museums.name: Centre Pompidou
museums.desc: A bold building with its pipes, stairs and ducts on the outside, painted in bright colors, holds Europe's biggest collection of modern and contemporary art, with huge holdings of Kandinsky, Matisse and Picasso.
museums.history: President Georges Pompidou wanted a big new cultural center for Paris, and an architecture contest in 1971 was won by Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers, who put the building's insides on the outside. Many Parisians hated it at first. It opened in 1977, almost three years after Pompidou's death, and has been one of the city's most popular sights since.

museums.name: Musée de l'Orangerie
museums.desc: Two oval rooms in the Tuileries Garden are wrapped with Claude Monet's giant Water Lilies panels, painted to give visitors a feeling of peace after the First World War.
museums.history: Monet offered the Water Lilies to France the day after the armistice of November 1918, as a gift of peace. He worked on them for years at Giverny, and designed the oval rooms in the Orangerie, a former greenhouse for orange trees. The museum opened in 1927, a few months after Monet died. A large collection of Impressionist and modern art was added in 1984.

museums.name: Musée Marmottan Monet
museums.desc: A small museum in a former hunting lodge in western Paris, which has the world's largest collection of Monet, including the painting Impression, Sunrise that gave Impressionism its name.
museums.history: Paul Marmottan, a collector of Napoleonic art, left his mansion and its collections to the Academy of Fine Arts in 1932 and it opened as a museum in 1934. In 1966 Monet's son Michel left it the paintings that remained in the artist's house, including many water lilies. Impression, Sunrise had come in 1940 as a gift. Thieves stole it in 1985, and it was found again in 1990.

museums.name: Palace of Versailles
museums.desc: The grandest royal palace in Europe, with its Hall of Mirrors and vast gardens, is also a museum of French history, with huge painted rooms of battles and kings.
museums.history: Louis XIV, the Sun King, turned his father's hunting lodge into a magnificent palace and moved the government of France there in 1682. The Hall of Mirrors was finished in the 1680s. After the French Revolution, the palace was left almost empty, until King Louis-Philippe turned it into a museum of French history in 1837. Many events happened here, including the signing of the treaty that ended the First World War in 1919.

museums.name: Petit Palais
museums.desc: A little palace with a gorgeous garden courtyard near the Champs-Élysées, built for the 1900 World's Fair and now the City of Paris's Museum of Fine Arts, free to enter.
museums.history: The Petit Palais was built by Charles Girault for the Exposition Universelle of 1900, along with the Grand Palais opposite. It became a museum for the city's collections in 1902. It holds works by Courbet, Monet, Delacroix and many Paris painters, and its building is one of the best examples of 1900 Beaux-Arts architecture.

museums.name: National Gallery
museums.desc: On Trafalgar Square in the center of London, a free museum shows Western European painting from about 1250 to 1900, including Van Gogh's Sunflowers, Constable's Hay Wain and Turner's Fighting Temeraire.
museums.history: The government bought 38 paintings from the collection of a banker, John Julius Angerstein, in 1824 to start the National Gallery, and it first showed them in his house on Pall Mall. The present building on Trafalgar Square, by William Wilkins, opened in 1838. During the Second World War the paintings were hidden in a Welsh slate quarry, and a single painting was shown each month in London. Entry is free.

museums.name: Tate Britain
museums.desc: The national collection of British art from 1500 to today stands on the bank of the Thames, with the world's biggest collection of J. M. W. Turner, as well as Pre-Raphaelites like Millais and Rossetti.
museums.history: Sir Henry Tate, a sugar tycoon, gave his collection and money for a building to the nation, and the National Gallery of British Art opened in 1897 on the site of an old prison at Millbank. It was known as the Tate Gallery for many years. Turner left a huge number of his paintings and sketches to the nation, and a special gallery for them, the Clore Gallery, was added in 1987. It became Tate Britain in 2000, when the modern art moved to Tate Modern.

highlights.title: Snow Storm: Steam-Boat off a Harbour's Mouth

museums.name: Tate Modern
museums.desc: A giant former power station on the Thames, with a tall brick chimney, is now one of the world's most popular modern art museums, with a huge hall, called the Turbine Hall, for large installations.
museums.history: Bankside Power Station was built in the 1940s and 1950s and closed in 1981. The Tate chose it as the home for its collection of international modern art in 1994, and the architects Herzog & de Meuron made it into a museum that opened in 2000. A new building, called the Blavatnik Building, opened in 2016. Free to enter, it receives millions of visitors each year.

museums.name: The Courtauld Gallery
museums.desc: A small gallery in Somerset House with one of the most beautiful collections of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist paintings in the world, including Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère and Van Gogh's Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear.
museums.history: The textile businessman Samuel Courtauld bought Impressionist paintings when they were still unpopular in Britain and, in 1932, helped to found the Courtauld Institute of Art to study art history. He gave his collection to the institute. Since 1989 the gallery has been in Somerset House, a grand building by the Thames, and it reopened after a big renovation in 2021.

museums.name: The Wallace Collection
museums.desc: A free museum in a grand house in Manchester Square, packed with French 18th-century painting, porcelain and armor. Its most famous painting is Fragonard's The Swing.
museums.history: The collection was put together by four generations of the Marquesses of Hertford and by Sir Richard Wallace, who inherited it in 1870. His widow, Lady Wallace, left it to the British nation in 1897 on condition that it be kept in London, and it opened to the public in 1900 in Hertford House.

museums.name: Scottish National Gallery
museums.desc: A neoclassical gallery on the Mound in the center of Edinburgh holds fine European and Scottish paintings, including Raeburn's Skating Minister.
museums.history: The National Gallery of Scotland opened to the public in 1859, in a building designed by William Henry Playfair, with Prince Albert laying the foundation stone in 1850. It grew through gifts and has works by Scottish painters such as Henry Raeburn, Allan Ramsay and David Wilkie. Entry is free.

museums.name: Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery
museums.desc: A grand Victorian museum in the heart of Birmingham, which has one of the world's best collections of Pre-Raphaelite paintings, and also the Staffordshire Hoard of Anglo-Saxon gold.
museums.history: The museum opened in 1885 in a splendid building in Chamberlain Square, paid for with Victorian city money. Its Pre-Raphaelite collection grew because the city's own artists, including Edward Burne-Jones, born in Birmingham, were admired locally. In 2009 the Staffordshire Hoard, the largest hoard of Anglo-Saxon gold ever found, was discovered and brought here.

museums.name: Imperial War Museum London
museums.desc: Britain's national museum of modern war has a very large art collection, including works by official war artists such as John Singer Sargent, Paul Nash and Wyndham Lewis.
museums.history: The Imperial War Museum was started in 1917 while the First World War was still going on, to record the war for later generations. The government hired top artists as war artists and their work is still the heart of the art collection. It moved in 1936 to a building that was a former hospital for people with mental illness, in Lambeth. Sargent's Gassed hangs here.

highlights.title: We Are Making a New World

museums.name: Uffizi Gallery
museums.desc: The world's top museum of Renaissance art is in a long Florentine palace beside the Arno river, with Botticelli's Birth of Venus and Primavera, works by Leonardo, Raphael and Michelangelo, and a priceless collection of Italian masters.
museums.history: The word uffizi means offices. Cosimo I de' Medici had the building put up in 1560 to hold the government's offices, and the Medici family used the top floor to display their art from about 1581. The last Medici, Anna Maria Luisa, left everything to the city of Florence in 1737 on condition that it never leave Tuscany, which is why the masterpieces are still there. The gallery opened to the public in 1769. In 1993 a bomb damaged part of the building, and many paintings were repaired.

museums.name: Vatican Museums
museums.desc: The collections of the popes include the Sistine Chapel with Michelangelo's ceiling and the Raphael Rooms, which hold The School of Athens. They are among the most visited art museums in the world.
museums.history: The museums began in 1506 when Pope Julius II put the newly discovered ancient statue of Laocoön on display in the Vatican. Over the centuries, successive popes added ancient sculptures and paintings, and the museums opened to the public in the late 1700s. Michelangelo painted the Sistine ceiling between 1508 and 1512 for Julius II, and Raphael painted the rooms around 1509 to 1520.

museums.name: Pinacoteca di Brera
museums.desc: Milan's great painting gallery holds masterpieces of northern Italian art by Mantegna, Bellini, Raphael and Caravaggio, in a palace that also houses an art academy.
museums.history: Napoleon, who was ruling northern Italy, founded the Brera gallery in 1809 as a place where students at the art academy could study great paintings, many of them taken from churches that had been closed. The palace was built in the 1600s by the Jesuits. Its best known painting for visitors is Hayez's The Kiss, bought for the museum in the 1860s.

museums.name: Gallerie dell'Accademia
museums.desc: Venice's top art gallery shows Venetian painting from the 1300s to the 1700s in an old convent and charity house on the Grand Canal, with works by Bellini, Titian, Tintoretto and Veronese.
museums.history: Napoleon closed churches and charities in Venice, and the paintings from them were gathered in the buildings of the Accademia, which became a museum in 1817. The gallery uses the former Santa Maria della Carità, a church, school and monastery. It also owns Leonardo's famous drawing of the Vitruvian Man, though it is shown only occasionally.

museums.name: Galleria Borghese
museums.desc: A small museum in a palace in a Roman park, with the sculptures of Bernini, a large group of Caravaggio paintings and Titian's Sacred and Profane Love.
museums.history: Cardinal Scipione Borghese built the villa in the early 1600s as a place to show his art collection, and he supported the young sculptor Bernini and the painter Caravaggio. The building was reorganized in the 1700s, and the collection was acquired by the Italian state in 1902. It opened as a public museum in 1903. To keep it from becoming too crowded, visitors must book a two-hour time slot.

highlights.title: Boy with a Basket of Fruit

museums.name: Museo di Capodimonte
museums.desc: A royal palace on a hill above Naples with the Farnese collection, including masterpieces by Titian, Raphael and Caravaggio.
museums.history: King Charles of Bourbon began the palace in 1738, both as a hunting lodge and to house the art he had inherited from the Farnese family, which came from his mother. It became a museum of the Italian state in 1957 and is set in a huge royal park.

museums.name: Museo del Prado
museums.desc: The Prado is Spain's great museum, with the world's best collection of Velázquez and Goya, as well as Bosch, El Greco, Titian and Rubens. Most of its pictures once belonged to the kings of Spain.
museums.history: King Ferdinand VII and his queen, Maria Isabel, opened the museum in 1819 as a royal museum of paintings, in a neoclassical building by Juan de Villanueva that had been designed for a natural history museum. It became a national museum after the 1868 revolution. During the Spanish Civil War of 1936 to 1939, its paintings were moved to Valencia and Geneva for safety. A big extension opened in 2007.

museums.name: Museo Reina Sofía
museums.desc: Spain's national museum of modern art, in a former hospital in Madrid, is home to Picasso's Guernica, as well as works by Dalí, Miró and Juan Gris.
museums.history: The building was a big hospital from the 1700s, and it was converted into an art center in the 1980s. The museum opened in 1992. Guernica, Picasso's huge painting of the bombing of a Basque town in 1937, came to Spain from New York in 1981 after Picasso had said it should not go to Spain until the country was a democracy again.

museums.name: Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza
museums.desc: A palace on Madrid's Paseo del Prado holds a fine private collection that fills the gaps in the Prado, with paintings from the 1200s to the 1900s from Holbein and Caravaggio to Hopper and Hartley.
museums.history: Baron Hans Heinrich Thyssen-Bornemisza, one of Europe's great collectors, put together one of the best private collections of art in the 1900s. Spain rented it in 1988 and bought it in 1993, and it is shown in the Villahermosa Palace. His wife Carmen, a Spanish former beauty queen, helped to bring it to Madrid.

museums.name: Sorolla Museum
museums.desc: The house and studio of the painter Joaquín Sorolla, the great painter of Spanish sunshine, are now a little museum with a lovely garden in the middle of Madrid.
museums.history: Joaquín Sorolla built his house in 1910 and lived there with his family until he died in 1923. His widow, Clotilde, left the house and its paintings to the Spanish state, and it opened as a museum in 1932. Some of the garden was designed by Sorolla himself, in the style of Andalusian gardens.

museums.name: Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya
museums.desc: A grand palace on Montjuïc hill above Barcelona, famous for the best collection of Romanesque wall paintings in the world, rescued from tiny mountain churches of the Pyrenees.
museums.history: The Palau Nacional was built for the 1929 World's Fair in Barcelona. The museum was founded in 1934 and moved into the palace in the 1990s. Many of the Romanesque murals were cut from church walls in the early 1900s and moved to Barcelona to save them from being sold abroad.

highlights.title: Christ in Majesty from Sant Climent de Taüll

museums.name: Calouste Gulbenkian Museum
museums.desc: A peaceful modern museum in a garden in Lisbon holds the private collection of an Armenian oil businessman, with Egyptian, Islamic, European and Asian treasures.
museums.history: Calouste Gulbenkian, an Armenian oil businessman, spent most of his life in Britain and France and settled in Lisbon in 1942. When he died in 1955 he left his collection and his fortune to a foundation in Portugal, and the museum opened in 1969. His collection includes paintings by Rembrandt, Rubens, Monet and Renoir.

museums.name: Rijksmuseum
museums.desc: The national museum of the Netherlands holds the great art of the Dutch Golden Age: Rembrandt's Night Watch, Vermeer's Milkmaid and hundreds of other paintings of the 1600s, in a fairy-tale brick building with a cycle path running through it.
museums.history: The Dutch government founded a national art gallery in The Hague in 1800 and moved the collection to Amsterdam in 1808, where King Louis Napoleon, Napoleon's brother, made it a royal museum. The present red-brick building by Pierre Cuypers opened in 1885. A ten-year renovation closed most of the museum from 2003 to 2013, and it reopened to huge crowds. The Night Watch has its own room, and in 2019 a team began a public scientific restoration of it, which visitors can watch.

museums.name: Van Gogh Museum
museums.desc: The world's largest collection of Van Gogh's paintings and drawings, with about 200 paintings, is in a modern building beside the Rijksmuseum, along with his letters and works by his friends.
museums.history: After Vincent van Gogh's death in 1890, his brother Theo and then Theo's wife, Johanna van Gogh-Bonger, kept and promoted the art. Vincent's nephew, also named Vincent, a young engineer, agreed in 1962 that the Dutch state would build a museum for the collection. The Van Gogh Museum, designed by Gerrit Rietveld, opened in 1973. A new wing designed by Kisho Kurokawa opened in 1999.

museums.name: Mauritshuis
museums.desc: A small, elegant 17th-century mansion in The Hague holds some of the most famous paintings in the Netherlands: Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring, Rembrandt's Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Tulp and Fabritius's Goldfinch.
museums.history: Johan Maurits, a Dutch governor in Brazil, had the house built in the 1640s. It became a museum in 1822, when the Dutch government bought it to show the royal art collection. In 2014 it reopened after a two-year renovation and a new underground extension. Donna Tartt's novel The Goldfinch, from 2013, made one of its paintings famous.

highlights.title: The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp

museums.name: Kröller-Müller Museum
museums.desc: A museum in the middle of a big national park, with the second-largest collection of Van Gogh in the world, as well as works by Seurat and Mondrian and a great sculpture garden.
museums.history: Helene Kröller-Müller, who was the wife of a shipping tycoon, began to collect art in 1907 on the advice of an art teacher. She was among the first to buy Van Gogh's paintings in large numbers. In 1935 she gave her collection to the Dutch state, and the museum opened in 1938 in the woods of the Hoge Veluwe. The sculpture garden, one of the biggest in Europe, grew after the Second World War.

museums.name: Kunstmuseum Den Haag
museums.desc: The art museum of The Hague, in an elegant brick building by the architect Berlage, holds the largest collection of Piet Mondrian's work in the world, including his last paintings, Victory Boogie Woogie.
museums.history: The museum started in 1866 as a municipal collection and moved to a building by H. P. Berlage, which opened in 1935. Mondrian, who was Dutch, spent much of his life in Paris, London and New York, and his friend Salomon Slijper kept a big group of his paintings, which came to the museum in 1946, so that the museum could trace his path from landscapes to pure abstraction.

highlights.title: Composition with Large Red Plane, Yellow, Black, Grey and Blue

aliases: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium
museums.name: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium
museums.desc: A group of connected museums in the heart of Brussels, with Old Masters of the Low Countries, Rubens, Bruegel, Magritte, David's Death of Marat and a fine Belgian modern collection.
museums.history: Napoleon's government founded a museum in Brussels in 1801, which grew into the Royal Museums with a new neoclassical building in 1887. The Magritte Museum, with the world's biggest collection of the Belgian Surrealist René Magritte, was added in 2009. David came to Brussels when he was exiled from France after Napoleon fell.

highlights.title: Landscape with the Fall of Icarus

aliases: Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp
museums.name: Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp (KMSKA)
museums.desc: Antwerp's big museum has a collection of six centuries of Flemish art, from Jean Fouquet to Rubens and James Ensor, in a great building that reopened in 2022 after a long renovation.
museums.history: The museum has its roots in 1810, when Napoleon returned paintings that had been taken to Paris to Antwerp. It was housed in its present building from 1890 and was closed for 11 years for a restoration that ended in 2022. Rubens, who lived and worked in Antwerp, is the museum's star.

museums.name: Alte Pinakothek
museums.desc: One of the world's oldest and greatest galleries of Old Master paintings, with works by Dürer, Rubens, Rembrandt, Raphael and Leonardo, housed in a huge brick-red building in the museum quarter of Munich.
museums.history: King Ludwig I of Bavaria wanted to open the royal collections to the public, and he had the architect Leo von Klenze build the museum, which opened in 1836. It was one of the largest museums in the world when it was built, and many later galleries copied its design. It was badly damaged in the Second World War and rebuilt in the 1950s.

museums.name: Lenbachhaus
museums.desc: A villa in Munich with the world's most important collection of the Blue Rider group, including Kandinsky, Marc, Macke and Gabriele Münter, who brought their colors to modern art.
museums.history: The painter Franz von Lenbach built the Italian-style villa in 1887, and after his death it became a city gallery in 1929. In 1957 Gabriele Münter, Kandinsky's partner, gave the museum about a thousand works by Kandinsky and her friends that she had hidden from the Nazis. The villa was expanded with a golden-colored extension in 2013.

museums.name: Gemäldegalerie, Berlin
museums.desc: Berlin's collection of European paintings from the 1200s to the 1700s has Vermeer, Rembrandt, Bruegel, Dürer and Botticelli, in a sleek modern gallery at the Kulturforum.
museums.history: The collection began with the Prussian royal art collection, which was opened to the public in the Altes Museum in 1830. After the Second World War it was divided between East and West Berlin, and was reunited in 1998 in a new building. Many of its masterpieces had been hidden in mines and bunkers during the war.

museums.name: Alte Nationalgalerie
museums.desc: A temple-like gallery on Berlin's Museum Island, with German and French art of the 1800s: Caspar David Friedrich's Romantic paintings, Menzel, Böcklin and the Impressionists.
museums.history: The building was designed by Friedrich August Stüler and Johann Heinrich Strack and opened in 1876 for paintings of the 'present', 19th-century art, with the help of a donation by the banker Joachim Wagener. It was damaged in the Second World War and reopened in 2001 after a major restoration. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Museum Island.

highlights.title: Frederick the Great Playing the Flute at Sanssouci

museums.name: Hamburger Kunsthalle
museums.desc: Hamburg's art museum is known for German Romantic painting and holds Caspar David Friedrich's masterpiece, Wanderer above the Sea of Fog.
museums.history: The museum was founded by citizens of Hamburg and opened in 1869 in a building by Georg Theodor Schirrmacher and Hermann von der Hude. It has been extended several times, and a new cube-shaped building opened in 1997 for modern art. The Friedrich collection is its pride.

highlights.title: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog

museums.name: Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister (Dresden)
museums.desc: The Zwinger palace in Dresden houses a gallery of Old Masters that is home to Raphael's Sistine Madonna, famous for the two little angels at the bottom.
museums.history: The painting collection goes back to the 1500s and the rulers of Saxony, who were great collectors. In the 1740s Augustus III bought masterpieces including the Sistine Madonna. The Zwinger gallery was built in the 1850s by Gottfried Semper, and the paintings were hidden during the bombing of Dresden in 1945, then taken by the Soviet army and returned to Dresden in 1955.

highlights.title: Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window

museums.name: Städel Museum
museums.desc: Frankfurt's art museum holds 700 years of European art, from the Middle Ages to today, with work by Vermeer, Botticelli, Monet and Beckmann.
museums.history: The banker Johann Friedrich Städel left his art collection and fortune in 1815 to found an art institute, one of the first museums in Germany created by a private citizen rather than a ruler. The museum grew with gifts from citizens of Frankfurt. A garden hall for modern art was built beneath the museum's courtyard in 2012.

museums.name: Kunsthistorisches Museum
museums.desc: Vienna's great museum holds the Habsburg dynasty's art, including the world's largest collection of Pieter Bruegel the Elder, with his Tower of Babel and Hunters in the Snow, as well as Vermeer's Art of Painting.
museums.history: The Habsburg emperors, who ruled much of Europe, collected for centuries. Emperor Franz Joseph ordered a pair of matching museums to be built on the Ringstrasse, and the Kunsthistorisches Museum opened in 1891, facing a twin building for natural history. The sumptuous interior has paintings by Klimt in the stairwell.

museums.name: Belvedere
museums.desc: A pair of baroque palaces with beautiful gardens in Vienna, which hold the world's largest collection of Gustav Klimt, including The Kiss.
museums.history: Prince Eugene of Savoy, a famous general, had the Belvedere palaces built in the early 1700s. The imperial art collection was displayed here from 1781. Since 1903 the palace has also housed a modern gallery, which bought Klimt's The Kiss in 1908 straight from his studio, when it was first shown, for a huge sum.

museums.name: Leopold Museum
museums.desc: A modern white limestone cube in Vienna's MuseumsQuartier shows the largest collection of Egon Schiele paintings in the world, and important works by Klimt and Vienna's Secession artists.
museums.history: Rudolf Leopold, a doctor and collector, spent his life buying works by Egon Schiele when they were unfashionable. In 1994 the Austrian government bought his collection, with around 5,000 pieces, for a foundation, and the museum, designed by Ortner & Ortner, opened in 2001.

museums.name: Kunstmuseum Basel
museums.desc: The oldest public art collection in the world has Holbein and Cranach, Picasso and Klee in two buildings in the Swiss city of Basel.
museums.history: In 1661 the city of Basel bought the collection of the Amerbach family, the first time that a private art collection was bought for the public. That is why Basel's museum is said to be the oldest public art museum in the world. It has the world's biggest collection of the painter Hans Holbein the Younger, and its modern wing is famous for Picasso.

museums.name: Kunsthaus Zürich
museums.desc: Zürich's art museum holds the largest collection of Edvard Munch outside Norway, plus Monet, Giacometti and a big collection of Swiss art.
museums.history: The Zürich Art Society built the museum, designed by Karl Moser, which opened in 1910. The Swiss collection of Alberto Giacometti was added over time, and so was the Foundation E. G. Bührle Collection of Impressionist paintings in a 2021 extension by David Chipperfield.

museums.name: National Gallery Prague (Trade Fair Palace)
museums.desc: The national art museum of the Czech Republic has several buildings in Prague, and its big Veletržní Palace holds modern art of the 1800s and 1900s, with Czech painters, and Klimt, Schiele and Picasso.
museums.history: A group of Czech nobles founded a society to promote art in 1796, which led to the National Gallery. The modern art is housed in the Trade Fair Palace, a huge functionalist building of the 1920s, which became a gallery in 1995.

museums.name: National Museum in Warsaw
museums.desc: Poland's biggest art museum has Polish painting from the Middle Ages to today, with Jan Matejko's giant Battle of Grunwald, and also works from ancient Egypt and Europe.
museums.history: The museum was founded in 1862 while Poland was divided among foreign powers, as a place where Polish culture could be shown. Its modern building opened in 1938, but in the Second World War the Nazis looted and destroyed much of the collection. After the war many works were recovered, and the museum has restored Matejko's Battle of Grunwald, one of the largest paintings in Poland.

museums.name: National Museum in Kraków
museums.desc: Kraków's national museum has Polish art in the beautiful Cloth Hall in the main square, and it also includes the Czartoryski Museum, which holds Leonardo da Vinci's Lady with an Ermine.
museums.history: The museum began in 1879, when the city gave its collection a home, and its Gallery of 19th-Century Polish Art in the Cloth Hall in the main square opened in 1879. In 2016 the Czartoryski Foundation's collections were bought by the Polish state and joined the museum.

museums.name: The State Hermitage Museum
museums.desc: One of the largest art museums in the world fills the Winter Palace of the tsars and four other buildings on the Neva river, with about three million objects, including Rembrandt, Leonardo, Matisse and Picasso.
museums.history: Catherine the Great began the Hermitage in 1764 by buying a collection of 225 paintings from Berlin, and she kept adding to it, buying whole collections of European masters. It became a public museum only in 1852. After the revolution in 1917 the Winter Palace became part of the museum, and the Soviet government added art taken from private collectors, such as the Impressionists of Shchukin and Morozov. During the siege of Leningrad of 1941 to 1944 the staff hid the art and stayed in the basement.

highlights.title: The Return of the Prodigal Son

museums.name: State Tretyakov Gallery
museums.desc: The national gallery of Russian art, in a fairy-tale building in Moscow, holds the best of Russian painting, including Repin, Shishkin, Vrubel and Malevich's original Black Square.
museums.history: The Moscow merchant Pavel Tretyakov began buying Russian paintings in 1856 and decided to give them to the city. In 1892 he donated his collection of about 1,300 paintings, and the gallery opened to the public. Tretyakov's house was rebuilt with the folk-style facade by Viktor Vasnetsov. After the revolution it became a state museum.

highlights.title: Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan

museums.name: Pushkin Museum of Fine Arts
museums.desc: Moscow's main museum of European art has masterpieces by Botticelli, Rembrandt, Monet and Van Gogh, in a classical building near the Kremlin. It is named after the poet Alexander Pushkin.
museums.history: The museum was founded in 1912 by the professor Ivan Tsvetaev as a place for students to study casts of famous sculptures. After the revolution, the Soviet government gave it large collections of paintings seized from Russian collectors, including the Impressionist and modern paintings of Sergei Shchukin and Ivan Morozov, which the Pushkin Museum shares with the Hermitage.

museums.name: State Russian Museum
museums.desc: The world's biggest collection of Russian art is in an elegant palace in Saint Petersburg and has masterpieces by Repin, Aivazovsky, Bryullov and Kandinsky.
museums.history: Tsar Alexander III wanted a national museum of Russian art, and after his death in 1894 Tsar Nicholas II opened the Russian Museum in the Mikhailovsky Palace in 1898. It grew after the revolution, with gifts from famous painters. It's the home of Repin's Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks and Bryullov's Last Day of Pompeii.

aliases: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design
museums.name: Nasjonalmuseet (National Museum, Oslo)
museums.desc: Norway's national museum, the largest art museum in the Nordic countries, opened a vast new building on the Oslo waterfront in 2022. It has Munch's The Scream and the best paintings of Norway's fjords, mountains and troll tales.
museums.history: Norway founded its national gallery in 1837, soon after it became independent of Denmark in 1814, in order to show the new nation's art and culture. The collection was housed in several places. In 2022 the National Museum opened in a new building by the architect Klaus Schuwerk, on the harbor in Oslo, merging four museums into one, and it is the biggest museum building in the Nordic region.

museums.name: MUNCH (Munch Museum)
museums.desc: A tall, tilted museum on the Oslo waterfront holds the world's largest collection of Edvard Munch, about 28,000 works, including another version of The Scream.
museums.history: Edvard Munch left all the paintings, prints and drawings in his possession to the city of Oslo when he died in 1944. The Munch Museum opened in 1963 to mark the centenary of his birth. In 2021 it moved into a large new building on the Bjørvika waterfront, a 13-story tower of aluminum panels. In 2004 thieves stole The Scream and Madonna from the old museum, and the paintings were recovered two years later.

museums.name: Nationalmuseum
museums.desc: Sweden's national museum of art holds Rembrandt, Rubens, the Swedish painters Carl Larsson and Anders Zorn, and a famous Scandinavian design collection, in a Renaissance-style palace by the water.
museums.history: The Swedish king Gustav III opened the royal collection to the public as the Royal Museum in 1792, and the present building on Blasieholmen, designed by the German architect Friedrich August Stüler, opened in 1866. In 2018 it reopened after a five-year renovation. Carl Larsson's giant mural Midwinter Sacrifice was painted for its stairway in 1915.

museums.name: Statens Museum for Kunst (SMK)
museums.desc: Denmark's national gallery in Copenhagen has the best of Danish art, including the calm interiors of Hammershøi and Golden Age painters like Eckersberg, as well as European masters and Matisse.
museums.history: The Danish royal collections were opened to the public in 1827, and the present building on Sølvgade was finished in 1896. A modern extension by Anna Maria Indrio opened in 1998. The collection is full of paintings from the Danish Golden Age of the early 1800s.

museums.name: Ateneum
museums.desc: Finland's main art museum is in a lovely neoclassical building opposite Helsinki's railway station, with Finnish paintings of the Golden Age by Akseli Gallen-Kallela and Albert Edelfelt, as well as Van Gogh and Cézanne.
museums.history: The Ateneum was built in 1887 as the home of the Finnish Art Society, an art school and a museum in one. Finnish artists in the 1890s, such as Akseli Gallen-Kallela, found their national style in the Finnish folk epic, the Kalevala, and these paintings now hang here. The museum is part of the Finnish National Gallery.

museums.name: Skagens Museum
museums.desc: A museum at the northern tip of Denmark where the sea and sky meet, devoted to the Skagen Painters, a group of Scandinavian artists who painted summer light on the beach.
museums.history: Artists including P. S. Krøyer, Anna and Michael Ancher and Laurits Tuxen settled in the fishing village of Skagen in the 1870s and 1880s and painted the sea, the fishermen and the long summer evenings. They founded the Skagens Museum in 1908, and it opened in a yellow building on the town square. It holds the world's biggest collection of their work.

highlights.title: Summer Evening on Skagen's Southern Beach

museums.name: National Gallery of Ireland
museums.desc: Dublin's free national gallery has Irish and European art, including a lost Caravaggio that was found in a monastery dining room, and it has a big collection of paintings by Jack B. Yeats.
museums.history: The gallery opened in 1864 on Merrion Square. The writer George Bernard Shaw, who said the gallery had given him his education, left it a third of his royalties, and money from his play Pygmalion and the musical My Fair Lady paid for many purchases. In 1990 a missing Caravaggio, The Taking of Christ, was identified on the wall of a Jesuit house in Dublin and given to the gallery.

highlights.title: Lady Writing a Letter with Her Maid

museums.name: The Israel Museum
museums.desc: Israel's national museum sits on a hill in Jerusalem. It holds the Dead Sea Scrolls in the Shrine of the Book, archaeology of the Holy Land, Jewish art and a European art collection.
museums.history: The museum opened in 1965, designed by Alfred Mansfeld and Dora Gad, and its Shrine of the Book, built to house the Dead Sea Scrolls, is shaped like the lid of a jar in which the scrolls were found. The campus was renewed in 2010.

museums.name: Louvre Abu Dhabi
museums.desc: A museum under a huge silver dome by Jean Nouvel, on an island by the sea, that tells the story of human creativity across cultures, with a mix of ancient, medieval and modern art.
museums.history: France and the United Arab Emirates signed a deal in 2007 for a museum using the Louvre's name and expertise. The building by Jean Nouvel opened in 2017, with a dome of 7,850 metal stars that makes a 'rain of light'. Its collection includes Leonardo's La Belle Ferronnière on loan from Paris.

museums.name: Museum of Islamic Art, Doha
museums.desc: A bold geometric museum by I. M. Pei on its own island by Doha's waterfront, with manuscripts, ceramics, metalwork and textiles from three continents over 1,400 years of Islamic art.
museums.history: The architect I. M. Pei, then in his 90s, picked the site on the sea himself so that the museum could not be built in. It opened in 2008 and became one of the most important museums of Islamic art in the world.

museums.name: Tokyo National Museum
museums.desc: Japan's oldest and largest museum has the finest collection of Japanese art: samurai swords, ukiyo-e woodblock prints, screens, lacquer and Buddhist sculpture, in Ueno Park.
museums.history: The museum was founded in 1872, only a few years after Japan opened to the West, and began as an exhibition of the nation's treasures. Its present main building opened in 1938, and it also has the Gallery of Horyuji Treasures. It holds around 120,000 objects, including 89 National Treasures.

museums.name: National Palace Museum
museums.desc: A vast museum in Taipei holds around 700,000 pieces of Chinese imperial art, from jade and bronzes to calligraphy and paintings, that once belonged to the emperors in the Forbidden City.
museums.history: The Palace Museum opened in the Forbidden City in Beijing in 1925. When Japan invaded China, the treasures were packed in thousands of crates and moved around the country for 16 years. After the Chinese civil war, the Nationalist government took about 600,000 pieces to Taiwan in 1949, and the National Palace Museum opened in Taipei in 1965.

museums.name: The Palace Museum (Forbidden City)
museums.desc: The Forbidden City, the home of China's emperors for almost 500 years, is now a museum with more than a million objects of imperial art, including paintings, ceramics and clocks.
museums.history: Beijing's Forbidden City was built in 1406 to 1420 for the Ming emperor Yongle and was home to 24 emperors until the last emperor was forced out in 1924. The following year it became a museum. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the most visited museums in the world.

highlights.title: Along the River During the Qingming Festival

museums.name: Shanghai Museum
museums.desc: A museum in the shape of an ancient bronze vessel on People's Square, with fine Chinese bronzes, ceramics, calligraphy and paintings.
museums.history: It was founded in 1952, and moved in 1996 to its current building, a round-topped structure on a square base, which echoes the Chinese ideas of a round heaven and square earth. It is best known for its ancient bronzes and ceramics.

museums.name: Ohara Museum of Art
museums.desc: Japan's first museum of Western art, in the old merchant town of Kurashiki, has paintings by El Greco, Monet, Gauguin and Picasso.
museums.history: The businessman Magosaburo Ohara founded it in 1930 as a memorial to the painter Torajiro Kojima, who was sent to Europe to buy art for him. Kojima brought back Monet's Water Lily Pond and El Greco's Annunciation, among other works, and so people in rural Japan could see European art.

museums.name: National Museum of Western Art
museums.desc: Tokyo's museum for European art, in a building by Le Corbusier, holds Monet's water lilies, Rodin's Gates of Hell and works from the Renaissance to the 20th century.
museums.history: After the Second World War, France returned a collection of 375 works that the Japanese businessman Kojiro Matsukata had bought in Paris, on condition that a museum be built for them. Le Corbusier designed the museum, which opened in 1959 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

museums.name: National Gallery Singapore
museums.desc: The biggest collection of modern Southeast Asian art in the world, in two heritage buildings, the old Supreme Court and City Hall, in the centre of Singapore.
museums.history: Singapore turned its colonial City Hall and Supreme Court into a museum of Southeast Asian art, and it opened in 2015. The long process included joining the two buildings with a glass-and-steel roof.

museums.name: National Museum of Fine Arts (Philippines)
museums.desc: A neoclassical building in Manila, once the home of the legislature, holds Juan Luna's giant Spoliarium, the pride of the nation's art.
museums.history: Juan Luna won the gold medal at the 1884 Madrid exposition with his Spoliarium, a symbol for Filipinos of their struggle under Spain. The national museum now holds it in a hall that was once the Senate of the Philippines.

museums.name: National Gallery of Victoria
museums.desc: Australia's oldest and most visited art museum has Australian and international art, with its famous Great Hall and its stained-glass ceiling, and a wall of water at the entrance.
museums.history: The gallery was founded in 1861 in the gold-rush city of Melbourne, then one of the richest cities in the world. It moved to its present building by Roy Grounds in 1968. Its Great Hall has a stained-glass ceiling made by Leonard French.

aliases: Art Gallery of New South Wales
museums.name: Art Gallery of New South Wales
museums.desc: Sydney's art gallery sits above the harbour, with Australian, Aboriginal, Asian and European art.
museums.history: The gallery was founded in 1871 and opened in its neoclassical building in 1909. A new building by SANAA, called Sydney Modern, opened in 2022.

museums.name: National Gallery of Australia
museums.desc: Australia's national art collection in Canberra, with one of the world's largest collections of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art.
museums.history: Established in 1967 and opened to the public in 1982, the gallery has a collection of around 150,000 works. It bought Jackson Pollock's Blue Poles in 1973, which caused a political storm.

museums.name: Australian War Memorial
museums.desc: A museum and memorial in Canberra that has a big collection of official war art by Australian artists of both world wars and later.
museums.history: Charles Bean, a war correspondent of the First World War, planned the memorial, which opened in 1941. It has paintings by official war artists like George Lambert and Will Longstaff.

museums.name: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
museums.desc: New Zealand's national museum on the Wellington waterfront shows Māori treasures, the nation's natural history and art in a very hands-on way.
museums.history: Te Papa was formed in 1992 by combining the National Museum and the National Art Gallery, and opened at its current site in 1998. Its name means 'our place' in Māori, and Māori leaders have a say in the care of their taonga.

museums.name: Art Gallery of South Australia
museums.desc: Adelaide's art gallery has a fine collection of Australian art and a wide range of European works from the last five centuries.
museums.history: The gallery opened in 1881 and its present building dates from 1900. It runs the Adelaide Biennial of Australian Art.

museums.name: Egyptian Museum
museums.desc: A rose-colored building in Tahrir Square holds the largest collection of ancient Egyptian objects in the world, with around 120,000 items.
museums.history: The first museum of antiquities in Egypt was founded in 1835 to stop the export of its treasures. The present building opened in 1902. It had the treasures of Tutankhamun until they were moved to the Grand Egyptian Museum near the Giza pyramids.

aliases: Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa
museums.name: Zeitz MOCAA
museums.desc: The biggest museum of contemporary African art in the world is in a converted grain silo on Cape Town's waterfront, with a dramatic atrium cut into its concrete tubes.
museums.history: The grain silo, built in 1921, was once the tallest building in sub-Saharan Africa. The British architect Thomas Heatherwick turned it into a museum that opened in 2017.

museums.name: Iziko South African National Gallery
museums.desc: South Africa's national art gallery in Cape Town has South African, African and European art.
museums.history: It was founded in 1871 and has been in its present building since 1930. It is now part of the Iziko Museums of South Africa.

museums.name: Museum of Black Civilisations
museums.desc: A big circular museum in Dakar that tells the history and culture of Black and African peoples through art and objects.
museums.history: China helped to build the museum, which opened in 2018. It was designed to look like a traditional hut from the Casamance region, and it was created to bring back African art held in other countries.
